title: How Will AI Tools Like ChatGPT 4.0 and Notebook LM Shape the Future of Law? — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

st.t: AI writing: Present gains can weaken future judgment
st.an: The source supports supervised, user-controlled augmentation by depicting AI as an interactive editor whose suggestions require user approval and whose changes remain reversible. Its favourable account aligns with selective delegation, but it does not address verification costs, independent competence assessment or the risk of weakened future judgment.
qs: If you like its suggestion, you give it a thumbs up and it makes the change, right there in real time.

st.t: Everyday usability: Better formats do not prove accuracy
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition that accessible audio and collaborative drafting interfaces can encourage human-directed legal-AI use, while not proving accuracy or institutional readiness. Its evidence consists mainly of personal experiments, reported uses and prospective applications; it explicitly acknowledges unverifiable translation accuracy and uncertainty about law-firm or legal-department adoption.

Its reliance on personal experience rather than measured performance also aligns with the cluster’s caution that reported use cases are stronger evidence than broad transformation claims.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source accepts that AI-assisted drafting could increase legal-service capacity, while treating it as a complement to systemic reform rather than a sufficient solution to the justice gap. Its claims about productivity, wider service and faster decisions are prospective and qualitative, not evidence of sustained access gains.

kp.k: Human participation should persist throughout AI use
kp.d: Leonard advocates collaboration rather than handing professional functions entirely to AI, with human input spanning design, training, output testing and revision. McCormack endorses this human-in-the-loop approach. This is a normative recommendation, not evidence of how legal organisations currently supervise AI.
qs: So a strong AI policy and approach will always include a human in the loop.
make sure that we keep contributing our human input all along the way—from training and design and development through testing the outputs and revising and refining over time.

kp.k: Notebook LM enables source-grounded research and verification
kp.d: Leonard describes Notebook LM as a research assistant that synthesises user-uploaded materials, generates summaries and FAQs, answers document questions and supports brainstorming. Its clickable citations enable users to check assertions against source documents; she does not present this as a guarantee of accuracy. She reports support for 38 languages and describes YouTube processing as her understanding that it uses transcripts rather than watches videos. These are contemporaneous product descriptions, not independently tested legal-research findings.
qs: So once you upload whatever your content is into the notebook, that becomes the knowledge base for the AI to engage with you.
This Notebook LM actually has a citation feature, so you can go in and click and check on the source documents, make sure it’s accurate.
It currently supports 38 different languages.

kp.k: Audio interfaces may expand adoption and information processing
kp.d: Leonard reports that Notebook LM can turn uploaded content into a conversational podcast in two or three minutes, giving 50 documents as her tentative current limit. She attributes to Ethan Mollick the argument that this new interface generated enthusiasm for a product already available for a year. McCormack's experience listening to White House AI regulatory guidance illustrates a personal preference for audio over dense reading; Leonard also reports acquaintances using podcasts of public agency and congressional materials during commutes. These are anecdotes and a reported adoption argument, not measured comprehension gains.
qs: And it takes maybe two or three minutes, and at the end of it, you hear two people, like you and me, Bridget, talking back and forth about the content that you’ve uploaded.
So he makes the point that the way that we encounter artificial intelligence matters, with respect to adoption and uptake and creativity and all of those things.
And for me personally, it’s a better way to get information into my brain than just reading a really, really dry, dense document.

kp.k: Judicial audio preparation should supplement reading public briefs
kp.d: McCormack recounts suggesting that two judge friends upload briefs and listen to a generated discussion before oral argument. She explicitly conditions this example on publicly available, nonconfidential briefing and insists that listening cannot replace reading. This is a suggested supplementary workflow, not a report that the judges adopted it or achieved better outcomes.
qs: It’s all briefing that’s available on the website. There’s no confidential information.
Obviously, it’s not a substitute. They have to read the briefs, and they will read the briefs. There’s no shortcut.
But it might be a different way to engage with the issues in advance of preparing to talk to the lawyers about the case.

kp.k: Generated discussions could diversify legal education
kp.d: Building on a friend's hypothetical civil-procedure learning example, Leonard proposes uploading whole units of cases so generated discussions could compare courts' approaches across factual settings. She frames this as a more dynamic option for different learning preferences. McCormack also reports exploring audio versions of alternative-dispute-resolution educational materials. Neither provides evidence of improved student performance or professional competence.
qs: But if you were able to upload a whole unit of Civ Pro or torts or contracts and have the podcast sort of compare and contrast the different approaches that courts were taking in different factual circumstances—I think that would be really interesting.
This creates a little bit more of a dynamic learning environment.
We have so much educational material that you could imagine putting out in this new format for people who want to learn a little bit more about alternative dispute resolution.

kp.k: Research assistance could coordinate teams handling complicated records
kp.d: McCormack predicts benefits for lawyers, arbitrators, mediators and judges seeking a shared understanding of complicated records. Based on early experimentation, she says Notebook LM can assemble timelines and identify unclear areas. She likens its prospective role in transaction or litigation teams to an additional paralegal, an augmentation analogy rather than a claim of staffing displacement.
qs: I mean, I’ve only just started playing around with the back-and-forth Q&A you can do with Notebook LM.
It will put together a timeline and focus on, you know, specific places where there’s a lack of clarity.
And maybe a better tool for like a team of people that are working on the same complicated transaction or litigation—it’s just like adding a great additional super smart, really nice paralegal.

kp.k: Document conversations could help the public understand court proceedings
kp.d: Leonard anticipates members of the public uploading their case documents and asking questions to understand opinions, orders and what is happening in their cases. She presents this as a potential advance over earlier, manually intensive natural-language-processing approaches, not as demonstrated legal advice or successful case outcomes. Separately, she speculates that directed podcast discussions could arrive in years or perhaps months; at the time described, the podcast feature simply took a button click without user direction.
qs: I also think, you know, for the general public, there are huge opportunities to sort of leapfrog and make huge advances in natural language processing of documents that they get from a court—of trying to read judicial opinions or court orders and try and figure out exactly what’s actually happening with their case.

If you have a Notebook LM file and you can upload everything that you’ve had in a court case that you’re involved with and then ask it questions of the documents... I see that as being like a really exciting thing.
But I could see in the years ahead—maybe the months ahead at this rate—being able to direct the podcast hosts to focus on different elements of a case or set of cases.

kp.k: Canvas shifts drafting toward controlled, collaborative editing
kp.d: McCormack describes Canvas as an editable workspace combining conversation, a working document and editing functions: reading-level adjustment, inline suggestions, tone changes, final polish and version control. Leonard emphasises paragraph-level revision without regenerating satisfactory surrounding text. Both report that it feels like a writing partner with greater user control; Leonard explicitly distinguishes this experience from actual determinism, noting that output remains probabilistic.
qs: But what it is is basically an editable workspace that goes beyond the normal interaction you have with GPT-4.0 when you’re on the site.

It also has version control functions, so you can track your changes and you can revert to previous versions of all or part of it, so that you don’t lose track of something that maybe ends up not where you wanted it to end up in the editing process.

And so—even though it’s still a probabilistic generated output, which we’ve talked about before, is more of a guess as to the next word in a sequence—it feels a little bit closer to deterministic output because you have that control element.

kp.k: Usability could accelerate lawyers' uptake of AI
kp.d: McCormack predicts that Canvas's interface will encourage previously hesitant lawyers to adopt AI. Her presentation-drafting experience, including adapting text to her own voice, supports her account of rapid personal habit change, but is not evidence of profession-wide adoption. Leonard similarly locates the improvement partly in user engagement rather than necessarily in underlying technology.
qs: But it feels different to me. It feels like sort of a step up—not even necessarily in the technology—but in the user engagement and the facility with which you can sort of adapt your content.
But it's already, again, changed my habits that quickly, which is stunning.
It’s just got such a great user interface. I think it’s going to accelerate uptake.

kp.k: AI could expand legal aid and pro bono capacity
kp.d: McCormack predicts that controlled drafting assistance can help overstretched legal aid and community legal services organisations do more with limited staff and time. Leonard extends this to law-firm and corporate-department pro bono work, arguing that efficiency incentives differ from private hourly work and that technology can complement systemic reform. Her reference to '10X' productivity is aspirational rhetoric, not a measured result. McCormack proposes law-firm partnerships with community organisations to address larger unmet needs.
qs: I’m also excited about the ways that it might help legal aid organizations or community legal services organizations that have far more requests for help than they have time or hours or humans to provide that help.
because the business model for pro bono services in private sector legal work is so different, and you want to be as efficient as possible even if you’re always working on billable hour.

Or even better—it’s a really interesting opportunity for a forward-thinking law firm to partner with a community organization and bring this tech to bear on, you know, together handling a much bigger problem than either could probably tackle on its own.

kp.k: Judicial drafting assistance could relieve state-court workloads
kp.d: Responding to Leonard's question about faster decisions, McCormack reports that work she attributes to Adam Ulatekowski using Claude demonstrates good first drafts, especially for less complicated questions, clear precedent and few issues. She speculates that Canvas-style tools could support subsequent and final drafts. She sees particular value for heavily burdened state and intermediate appellate courts. The transcript supplies no study design, accuracy measures or measured time savings for these claims.
qs: the work he’s shown—just by using Claude—is that these models do a pretty great first draft, especially on legal questions that are maybe not as complicated, might be governed by pretty clear precedent, and not too many issues in the case.
But when you have this set of tools, it feels to me like it’s not only doing a great first draft—it’s maybe a great first, second, and final draft.
State appellate courts, intermediate appellate courts just have an unbelievable workload.

kp.k: Publicly available tools might narrow courts' technology disadvantage
kp.d: Leonard expresses hope that accessible AI will allow courts, not just corporate legal departments and law firms with advanced models, to improve the public's experience of dispute resolution and confidence in court systems. McCormack proposes collaboration between law firms and courts. These are prospective institutional opportunities, not demonstrated improvements in fairness, efficiency or public trust.
qs: But what gives me hope is maybe the court systems won’t be left behind this time—because we can actually figure out how to leverage the tools that are already publicly available to make people feel better about the outcomes in their cases.
Again—another really exciting collaborative opportunity for a law firm and a court to partner.

kp.k: Voice assistance suggests future action-taking workflows
kp.d: Leonard's personal meal-planning example illustrates conversational refinement of a recipe and shopping list through ChatGPT voice mode. She extrapolates to a future agent placing a grocery order on the user's behalf. This cross-domain example distinguishes demonstrated conversational assistance from speculative action execution; it does not establish a legal-service agent capability.
qs: It was perfect. Seamless.

as we develop more agents and more AI that can act on our behalf without us having to sort of do the things ourselves, I could imagine if you’re a grocery vendor, one day offering the option of just like, “Great, can you just put in that order for me and I’ll be right over to pick it up?”

kp.k: Generated application writing may undermine existing professional signals
kp.d: Reflecting on writing a recommendation, Leonard questions whether cover letters and written materials used for clerkships, bar admission and jobs will retain their value when compelling prose is easily generated. She raises possible changes in how content is consumed rather than asserting that selection practices have already changed.
qs: will these tools that we use even to apply for clerkships and bar admission and jobs continue to have the value that they have?
What value does a cover letter have in a world where any of us can snap our fingers and generate a cover letter that’s compelling and interesting?

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack describe Notebook LM as a research and record-processing assistant that could improve legal teams’ understanding of complicated materials.
pts.d: Leonard says the tool can rapidly synthesize uploaded sources and enable document-based questions with checkable citations. McCormack says it can create timelines and identify unclear parts of records, predicting that it could function as an additional team member on complex litigation or transactions. Her comparison to a paralegal describes augmentation, not a prediction of paralegal displacement.

pts.k: Both speakers anticipate new ways of learning and preparing for legal work through generated audio discussions.
pts.d: McCormack describes using podcasts to understand dense regulatory material and envisages alternative dispute resolution education in that format. She suggests judges could listen to discussions of case briefs as supplementary preparation. Leonard proposes podcasts comparing cases across a law-school unit, creating a more dynamic learning environment.

pts.k: Leonard predicts that document-based AI could help members of the public understand their court cases.
pts.d: She envisages people uploading case documents and asking questions to understand opinions, orders and developments in their own cases. This is a prospective public-facing legal comprehension benefit, not a demonstrated outcome or a claim that autonomous AI can replace counsel.

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack claim Canvas improves collaborative drafting control; McCormack predicts that its interface will accelerate lawyer adoption.
pts.d: They describe targeted paragraph editing, inline suggestions, tone changes and version control as improvements over regenerating entire responses. Leonard says this makes lawyers feel more in control, while expressly retaining the distinction between probabilistic generation and deterministic output. McCormack predicts the interface will encourage lawyers who have not yet adopted AI to use it.

pts.k: Both speakers predict greater legal aid and pro bono capacity through AI-assisted work and organizational partnerships.
pts.d: McCormack says Canvas could help resource-constrained legal services organizations accomplish more in less time. Leonard extends this to law-firm and corporate legal department pro bono work, where efficiency could increase the number of people served. McCormack proposes partnerships between firms and community organizations to address larger problems. Leonard's reference to tenfold productivity is aspirational rather than a measured result.

pts.k: McCormack predicts AI-assisted opinion drafting could improve court throughput; Leonard hopes publicly available tools could help courts and public confidence.
pts.d: Responding to Leonard's suggestion that AI could accelerate decisions, McCormack says models already produce useful first drafts for relatively straightforward cases and suggests Canvas-like editing could support subsequent and final drafts. She emphasizes busy state courts. Leonard expresses hope that publicly available technology will prevent courts from being left behind and improve people's experience of case outcomes. These are predictions and hopes, not reported court implementation results.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The research, learning and drafting claims principally rest on personal experimentation and informal reports.
pts.d: McCormack reports converting White House AI regulatory guidance into a podcast, trying Notebook LM's Q&A, and using Canvas for a presentation. Leonard describes her own targeted-editing experience and reports acquaintances converting public legal materials into commuter listening. The proposed student, judicial and public-facing applications extend these experiences; the transcript offers no controlled studies, quantified productivity measurements or legal accuracy benchmarks.

pts.k: McCormack supports the opinion-drafting claim by referring to another practitioner's work with Claude; broader capacity gains remain extrapolations.
pts.d: McCormack invokes work attributed in the transcript to Adam Ulatekowski, without presenting its methods, sample size or measured results. Her extension from first drafts to later drafts reflects her assessment of the new editing tools. Neither speaker supplies measured evidence for tenfold productivity, improved public confidence or increased numbers of legal aid clients served.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The discussion concerns publicly available tools at the time of the 2024 episode, with near-term predictions but no fixed implementation timetable.
pts.d: The speakers distinguish their experience with public products from uncertain in-house adaptations. Leonard predicts the ability to direct generated podcast discussions within years, possibly months, while noting that the version discussed only offered button-triggered generation without direction. McCormack expects court-efficiency applications to become attractive before too long. These relative timeframes should not be treated as descriptions of current product capabilities.

pts.k: Human participation, source checking and supplementary rather than replacement use qualify the envisioned applications.
pts.d: Leonard explicitly advocates a human-in-the-loop approach and identifies clickable source citations as a way to check accuracy. McCormack's proposal for judges concerns public, nonconfidential briefs and expressly does not replace reading them. Her strongest first-draft claim concerns less complicated legal questions with clear precedent and few issues. These qualifications frame the discussion primarily as augmentation.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Potential professional beneficiaries include legal teams, dispute-resolution professionals, students and judges.
pts.d: Lawyers and transaction or litigation teams could gain research, synthesis and drafting assistance; arbitrators and mediators could better navigate complex records; students could learn through comparative audio discussions; judges could supplement preparation and draft opinions more efficiently. McCormack particularly emphasizes state appellate workloads. The transcript does not predict staffing reductions or changes in associate leverage.

pts.k: Public-facing beneficiaries could include underserved legal clients and people trying to understand court documents.
pts.d: Legal aid and community legal services organizations could expand capacity despite limited resources. Law firms and corporate legal departments could serve more people through pro bono programs and partnerships. Members of the public could ask questions of their case materials, while courts could potentially improve the timeliness and experience of dispute resolution. These are proposed access-to-justice benefits rather than enterprise cost-saving findings.
